p.s: Pricing products from suppliers without MAP

p.t: If the supplier sets no minimum price, sell for **at least 2 times what you pay** them.
If the maker sets a minimum advertised price (the lowest price you may show), **follow that price**.
Never win by undercutting rivals. **Price wars** leave everyone with less profit.
Before paying for ads on a product, **check the market price**. If the profit is thin, skip paid ads.
Do not offer price matching for products from suppliers that set no minimum price.
Core floor: 2x wholesale for non-MAP products
p.s: Pricing products from suppliers without MAP

p.t: MAP means Minimum Advertised Price, the lowest price the maker lets you show publicly.
Non-MAP means no such price is set. Wholesale means the price you pay the supplier. The floor means the lowest price you should go below.
Without a MAP, set your selling price at **at least 2x wholesale**, which means twice what you pay. Competitors should also sell at a minimum of 2x wholesale.
For example, a 250 wholesale price implies a competitor price of at least 500.
The rule for non-MAP pricing is to set prices at **at least 2x wholesale**. Research competitor prices, meaning what other sellers charge.
If competitors sell above 2x, match or exceed that level rather than undercutting, which means selling a little cheaper than them.
Without a MAP or MSRP (the Manufacturer's Suggested Retail Price, the price the maker recommends), the formula is: **selling price = wholesale × 2**.
Example: wholesale 500 gives a selling price of 1,000. [L969.002]
Minimum advertised price for suppliers without a stated MAP: **MAP = 2 × wholesale cost**.
Example: wholesale $500 means the selling price should be at least $1,000, which leaves roughly 20 to 30% after expenses.
MAP means Minimum Advertised Price.
The 2x test: the **average competitor selling price** should be at least double the wholesale cost.
If it is below double, treat it as a red flag (a warning sign) and do not upload the supplier's product, since margins (the money you keep per sale after costs) will not be sustainable.

Example with $500 wholesale: an average competitor price of $700 fails the 2x test, so the product should not be listed. An average competitor price of $2,000 passes, leaving about **$1,500** per sale before fees.

p.t: Where a manufacturer sets a minimum advertised price, follow the MAP price list.
Where none exists, apply a **fixed markup** (a set amount added on top of cost), such as 20%, to each product and compare it with competitor prices. (Older advice, 2021-22.
This 20% fixed markup differs from the 2x floor above. Use the MAP list where one exists, and use the 2x floor for non-MAP products as described above.)

Put the pricing rule on the **upload card** (the form used to add a product to the store) so the person uploading does not have to guess.

**The sale price** (the price the customer actually pays) is the MAP.

p.t: The sources disagree on this case. Each applies to a different situation.

**L969.002**: Still list at a minimum of 2x. Rely on free traffic instead of paid ads.
**(undated)**: Treat it as a red flag and do not upload the product.
**step 3**: Do not run Google ads for the product. List it only if needed for catalog completeness.
**L855.046 (2023)**: List it at about double wholesale without ads. This keeps the store looking established.
**L966.049 step 3 and step 4 (2025)**: Keep it at a markup you accept and exclude it from paid ads.
Choose the option that fits your margin. If the product cannot reach an acceptable margin at the market price, the sources mainly differ on **whether to list it at all**.
Do not win non-MAP sales by undercutting competitors.
Price cuts start a **race to the bottom**, a cycle where sellers keep cutting prices until no margin is left.
Match the average market price when margins allow it, and win customers through conversion optimization (improving the store so more visitors buy) instead.
Sell at MAP and do not manipulate feed prices. Feed prices are the prices sent to shopping sites through your product feed, the file listing your products.
For non-MAP suppliers, match a low competitor price **only when profit remains**, because price wars leave everyone with less profit. [L469.071]
Pricing far below the market, for example selling a $1,000 market product at $800, starts a price war and gives away profit. **Price with the market** instead.

Using the three-times rule without checking the market can leave money on the table, because the actual market price may be much higher than three times wholesale. **Always check competitor prices first.**
With a strong review history, meaning many good customer ratings, a store can sell above MAP and still win sales.
A small discount, such as $50 off a multi-thousand-dollar order, can close the sale when buyers want peace of mind. [L806.055]

Escaping restrictions with your own brand
p.s: Pricing products from suppliers without MAP

p.t: Creating your own brand from a no-name supplier product (an unbranded product) lets you avoid pricing
and channel restrictions, meaning rules on price and on where you may sell.
Once you have a private brand with no restrictions, you can consider other sales channels, but only after the main store is **consistently strong**. [L357.043]
If a supplier does not enforce MAP, combine multiple units into **bundles**, meaning several items sold together as one,
and advertise them as a combo product. Build a separate product page for each bundle. [L852.054]
Combine the best-rated components from several suppliers, each already sold separately by its maker,
into **one starter kit** under your own brand. Offer a recurring consumables subscription on top. Consumables are items that get used up and need buying again.
Pattern: take the top-liked part from brand A, the kit from brand B and the consumable from brand C.
White-label each, which means having each maker's item sold under your brand name, then sell them as one bundle plus a subscription.

Example 1: a home brewing store white-labels a fermenter (a vessel where drinks ferment) from one maker, a kit from another and a yeast refill from a third. It sells a starter set with **monthly yeast delivery**.

Example 2: a coffee gear store white-labels a grinder, a brewing dripper (a cone that holds coffee and filter paper) and a filter paper pack into one starter bundle, with a **monthly filter subscription**.
A store selling 3D printers ran for about one year.

Customer comments showed that buyers liked the extruder (the part that pushes plastic into the printer) from one maker, the kit from another and the filament (the plastic thread the printer melts) from a third.
The owner planned to ask each maker to white-label its part, combine the parts into one starter bundle under the store's own brand, and add a filament subscription.
The owner sold the store **before this plan was carried out**.
